phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b] released straight into the lateral [l]; the cluster is as plain as English 'blow'.
Short open back rounded [ɔ], as in British English 'lot'; unstressed and brief.
Voiced dental stop [d] into the Welsh diphthong eu [ɛu̯], a glide from open e toward a close rounded vowel; this syllable carries the stress, as Welsh stresses the penult.
Labial-velar glide [w], short open [ɛ], and final Welsh dd [ð], the voiced dental fricative of English 'this' — never a stopped d.

pronunciation.approximation: 'blo-DEH-weth' — three syllables with the weight on the middle one; the final dd is the soft th of 'this', and the eu slides like the vowel of 'say' pulled toward a rounded close.

pronunciation.note: Blodeuwedd is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: Middle Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet and the manuscript spelling carries no diacritic or distinctive letter for ASCII to lose, so the restored form differs from the input only by the capital. The name is a transparent Welsh compound — blodau 'flowers' + gwedd 'face' — and its history runs in a circle: coined in the tale for a woman made of blossoms, it survives in modern Welsh as the everyday word for the owl she became.

domains.title: Flower Bride, Betrayal
domains.subtitle: The domain of Blodeuwedd
domains.lead: In the celtic tradition, Blodeuwedd is the flower-bride of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi: the fairest woman ever seen, made by [[gwydion|Gwydion]] and [[math|Math]] from the blossoms of oak, broom, and meadowsweet to defeat the destiny that barred Lleu Llaw Gyffes from every wife on earth — and the bride who loved Gronw Pebr of Penllyn, drew her husband's death-secret out of him, and was judged into the shape of the owl.

cards.name: Oak, Broom, and Meadowsweet
cards.desc: The three blossoms Math and Gwydion took up with their wands and fashioned into the fairest woman anyone had seen — a wife made by craft for the man no earthly wife was allowed.

cards.name: The Impossible Conditions
cards.desc: Neither in a house nor out of one, neither on horseback nor on foot — the death-terms Blodeuwedd drew from Lleu for Gronw: one foot on a cauldron's rim, one on a goat, a spear a year in the forging.

cards.name: The Owl
cards.desc: Gwydion's sentence — 'I will not kill you': the bird-shape hated by all birds, never to show its face by day, and the name Blodeuwedd kept as the mark of shame.

cards.name: Llyn y Morwynion
cards.desc: The Lake of the Maidens, where Blodeuwedd's attendants, looking backward as they fled through the mountains by night, walked into the water and drowned.

symbols.name: Oak, broom, and meadowsweet
symbols.meaning: The three flowers of her making — beauty assembled by enchantment, with no childhood and no kin

symbols.name: The spear a year in the forging
symbols.meaning: Worked only during Mass on Sundays — the weapon shaped by the stolen secret of an impossible death

symbols.name: The cauldron and the billy-goat
symbols.meaning: The two footings of the fatal stance: one foot on the rim, one on the beast — neither indoors nor out, neither mounted nor afoot

symbols.name: The owl
symbols.meaning: The shape of the sentence: the face that must not be shown by day, mobbed by every other bird

symbols.name: Llyn y Morwynion
symbols.meaning: The Lake of the Maidens — the backward glance in the dark that drowned her whole retinue

symbols.name: Mur Castell
symbols.meaning: Her court in Ardudwy, the bridal seat from which the hunter of Penllyn was welcomed in

mythology.lead: Blodeuwedd exists in exactly one witness, and it is enough: the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, 'Math uab Mathonwy', the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose. She enters the tale as its most beautiful artefact and leaves it as its most haunting sentence — a woman made from flowers, a bride who chose her own lover, and an owl that still bears her name in modern Welsh.

myths.title: Made of Flowers
myths.text:
When Arianrhod, shamed by the birth the wand had forced from her, laid her third destiny on her son — that he should never have a wife of any race then on earth — Math the king took counsel with [[gwydion|Gwydion]]: 'Let us try, by charms and enchantment, to conjure a wife for him out of flowers.' They took the flowers of the oak, the flowers of the broom, and the flowers of the meadowsweet, and from them made the fairest and most beautiful woman anyone had ever seen; they baptized her in the manner of the time, and named her Blodeuwedd, Flower-face.

The wedding sealed the counter-spell: Lleu was given the cantref of Dinoding to rule, and the pair settled at his court in Ardudwy, at the place called Mur Castell. The Fourth Branch gives the marriage one sentence of happiness — everyone was content — before it sets the trap the whole tale has been building toward: a king's nephew with a destiny, and a wife who was never born of woman at all.

myths.title: Gronw of Penllyn
myths.text:
Lleu went to Caer Dathyl to visit Math, and while he was away Gronw Pebr, the lord of Penllyn, came hunting into the country. At nightfall Blodeuwedd welcomed the hunter into the court — the hospitality owed to a guest — and the tale says simply that that night they talked, and she conceived a love for him, and he for her. Three nights they lay together while her husband sat at his uncle's court.

The Fourth Branch wastes no breath condemning them; it reports desire with the same flat care it gives to flower-making. But the lovers' question is the tale's hinge: how can they be together for good? Blodeuwedd's answer is to learn what only a wife can learn — the manner of her husband's death — and the text lets her do it in his own trust, 'in the guise of concern', asking how a man so strangely fated could ever be killed.

myths.title: The Impossible Conditions
myths.text:
Lleu, trusting, told her everything. He cannot be killed indoors or out of doors, on horseback or on foot. He can be killed only in one posture: a bath prepared on the bank of a river, a thatched frame over the tub, one foot on the rim of the cauldron and the other on the back of a billy-goat — and only by a spear worked for a full year, and only during the hours of Mass on Sundays. Blodeuwedd sent every word to Gronw, and Gronw set the smiths to work.

When the year was out she asked her husband to show her the marvellous stance — she would never understand it, she said, unless she saw it. The bath was drawn, the frame thatched, the goat brought; Lleu set one foot on the cauldron's rim and one on the goat, and Gronw rose from the hill called Bryn Cyfergyr and cast the spear. It struck Lleu in the side so the shaft stood out of him and the head stayed in, and with a terrible scream he flew up in the shape of an eagle and was gone. Gronw took the lands, and the flower-bride's making came to its harvest.

myths.title: The Lake of the Maidens
myths.text:
When Math and Gwydion came against Gronw, Blodeuwedd heard of it and fled with her maidens into the mountains. But fear made them walk backward, looking always behind them for the pursuit, until the whole company walked into a lake and drowned — all of them except Blodeuwedd herself. The tale names the place for them: Llyn y Morwynion, the Lake of the Maidens.

Gwydion overtook her in the mountains and took her. The image the Fourth Branch leaves is among the coldest in Welsh literature: the made woman fleeing through the dark with her dead companions behind her under the water, caught at last not by a warrior but by the enchanter who had fashioned her out of blossoms three years — or one lifetime — before.

myths.title: The Owl's Sentence
myths.text:
Gwydion's judgement is the Fourth Branch's second great transformation-sentence, and it is precise: 'I will not kill you; I will do what is worse. I will let you go in the shape of a bird. Because of the dishonour you have done Lleu Llaw Gyffes, you shall never dare show your face in the light of day, and that shall be from fear of all birds: they shall mob you and molest you wherever they find you. And you shall not lose your name, but shall always be called Blodeuwedd.' She went, in the shape of the owl. The tale adds its own etiology: blodeuwedd is what the owl is called to this day, and for that reason the birds hate the owl wherever it is found.

The aftermath belongs to the slain man's healing and the standing stone: Lleu, nursed back from eagle-shape and skin and bone, demanded to stand where Gronw had stood; Gronw took the stone slab between himself and the spear, and Lleu's cast drove through the slab and through him. The pierced stone on the bank of the Cynfael was called Llech Ronw, Gronw's stone. Blodeuwedd alone of the tale's dead is not buried — she is still flying, under her flower-name, in every Welsh word for owl.

lore.syncretism: Blodeuwedd's closest comparative kin is the made bride. Greek tradition offers [[pandora|Pandora]], the woman the gods fashion as a gift that is also a trap — beauty assembled by divine craft and given to a man, with ruin in the giving. The parallel holds at the level of motif, not borrowing: both figures are manufactured women whose makers intend one destiny and whose own desires rewrite it, though Pandora's makers send her as the trap while Blodeuwedd's makers are her undoing's victims. Within Celtic scholarship she has been read in the sovereignty frame — Mac Cana and others note the pattern by which the woman's favour carries the land, since Gronw takes Lleu's rule with his wife — and her triple flowers have drawn the attention of the tree-calendar speculation around Robert Graves, which the handbooks do not accept. The honest verdict is that she belongs to the international faithless-bride and made-woman complexes, with a sentence that is the Mabinogi's own: no other tradition punishes a woman by letting her keep her name forever.
lore.culturalLegacy: Blodeuwedd's afterlife is carried in two forms: a word and a novel. The word is blodeuwedd itself — in modern Welsh simply 'owl', so that every Welsh speaker who names the bird repeats her sentence, a folk-etymology the Fourth Branch deliberately installed. The novel is Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967), winner of the Carnegie Medal, which takes the Fourth Branch's triangle as a pattern that replays down the generations of a Welsh valley: a dinner service whose painted flowers resolve into owls, and three young people cast again as the flower-bride, the lord, and the hunter. The tale has become a set text of Welsh education and a touchstone of Welsh-language letters — retold for children, staged, and argued over by critics who read her as traitor, as sovereignty figure, or as the literature's first portrait of a made thing demanding a will of its own. In scholarship she holds a fixed place: Ifor Williams's edition, Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi, and Koch's encyclopedia all treat her episode as the Fourth Branch's tragic heart.
lore.extendedMeditation: Blodeuwedd is the Mabinogi's argument about what making means. Math and Gwydion make a woman the way they make illusions — by craft, for a purpose, to defeat a destiny — and the Fourth Branch's quiet question is what a made thing owes its makers. She has no mother, no father, no childhood, no choice in her marriage; she is given beauty, a name, a husband, and a court, and the tale watches, without comment, as the one thing she chooses for herself is a man and a murder. Gwydion's sentence is exact in its cruelty: not death, which would end her, but the kept name — Flower-face worn forever on the face of the night-bird every other bird hates. The punishment preserves her even as it damns her. Seven centuries later the word for owl in Welsh is still her name: the flowers never stopped blooming in it, and the shame never left it either.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Blodeuwedd (also written Blodeuedd), in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1400), the two codices of the Mabinogion. The normalized spelling is plain ASCII, so the restoration recovers no diacritic or distinctive letter — hence Tier 2, and the capital alone marks the temple form. The plain-ASCII domain blodeuwedd.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release; no form of the name is owned, and this temple claims none, standing at its canonical lexicon address in the meantime.

lore.archaeology: Blodeuwedd is a literary figure with no material cult record: no inscription, image, or votive object names her, and her witnesses are the two Mabinogion codices — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1400). What she has instead of temples is topography, and the Fourth Branch's map is still walkable. Mur Castell, her bridal court, is traditionally placed at Tomen y Mur in Ardudwy, beside the Roman fort; Llyn y Morwynion, the Lake of the Maidens where her retinue drowned, is pointed out above Ffestiniog; and on the bank of the river Cynfael stands a holed stone locally called Llech Ronw, 'Gronw's stone', the slab Lleu's spear pierced. These are local identifications rather than proof, but they show how early and how firmly the tale was staked into the landscape of Gwynedd — medieval hearers, like modern walkers, could be taken to the places where it happens.
